result: The study recruited 15 experts in EVD epidemiology through convenience and snowball sampling, conducted 40 interviews from November 2019 to March 2020, and used a structured elicitation methodology (roulette method) to collect expert forecasts. Two mathematical models (gravity and adjacency) were developed using spatiotemporal modeling approaches and fitted to 60 days of historical data.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised the methodology, with one stating 'A strength of the analysis is use of consistent methodology to elicit predictions from experts during an outbreak that can be compared to observations, and that are comparable to predictions from the models.' No concerns were raised about the study design or data collection procedures.

result: Expert forecasts showed mixed accuracy across months: correctly identifying Mabalako as highest-risk in December (82% probability, 38 actual cases), but underestimating Beni in January (0% probability of exceeding 20 cases despite this occurring), and accurately predicting Beni in February (70% probability of exceeding 6 cases, 9 actual cases). No cases were reported in March.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these descriptive findings without challenge. One reviewer summarized: 'Their key result concerned predicted numbers of cases in a defined set of zones. They found that neither the ensemble of models nor the group of experts produced consistently better predictions.' The specific monthly results are treated as factual observations.

result: Individual expert performance varied (Brier scores 0-0.6), with experts performing best at the highest threshold (20 cases) and worst at the lowest (2 cases). The gravity model ranked best at the two-case threshold, outperforming experts overall at this threshold. Both models performed particularly poorly in March compared to experts. No expert performed consistently well across all forecasts.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed these comparative findings, stating 'neither model performed consistently better than the other, and no expert's predictions were consistently better than the others.' The editor noted 'The evidence supporting the conclusions is convincing.' No methodological concerns were raised about the Brier score analysis.

result: Experts systematically over-predicted risk at the lowest threshold (≥2 cases) and under-predicted risk at the highest threshold (≥20 cases), with this bias present in 12 of 15 experts. Models showed no clear, consistent directional bias.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these bias findings without challenge. The systematic nature of expert bias is implicitly acknowledged in reviewer discussions of forecast performance patterns. No concerns were raised about the bias analysis methodology or interpretation.

result: When experts nominated additional health zones beyond the default list (7 zones in December), they consistently outperformed models in identifying flare-ups. The gravity model performed comparably to some experts in December and February, but the adjacency model performed worse than all experts except in February. Expert ensembles outperformed models in every month, and including models in ensembles reduced performance.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed this finding, stating 'Experts were also able to specify other zones in which they expected to see cases in the next month. For this part of the analysis, experts consistently outperformed the models.' This is treated as a key result distinguishing expert capabilities from model performance.

result: Expert ensembles performed similarly to the two models overall. Experts showed stronger bias than models at the two-case threshold, but both performed better at higher thresholds. Models were better at risk-ranking areas than experts. No individual expert outperformed ensembles overall, while models showed more consistent performance across forecasts.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these comparative performance findings, with one stating 'They found that neither the ensemble of models nor the group of experts produced consistently better predictions.' The editor affirmed 'The evidence supporting the conclusions is convincing.' No concerns were raised about these comparative analyses.

result: The authors claim this is the first study to record experts' assessment of geographical risk at a local level during an epidemic and the first real-time comparison of outbreak response experts' predictions to models.
evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accepted the novelty claim, with one stating 'Both individual experts and mathematical models are commonly used to support outbreak response, but the relative strengths of each information source are rarely quantified.' Another noted this provides 'an in-depth analysis' that is 'important and unique.'

result: The study has several limitations: it began only in the closing phase of the epidemic, which may have affected relative performance of experts versus models; the trend toward negative results may have favored certain forecasting methods; experts were interviewed on different days with varying information availability; and experts may have been influenced by existing model outputs.
evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about these limitations. One noted 'The elicitation was performed in four months near the end of the outbreak' and that 'The comparison of models to experts may therefore not be applicable to early stages of an outbreak when expert opinions may be less well-tuned.' Another stated 'forecast performance is known to be inconsistent and unpredictable across many dimensions' and emphasized the need to 'replicate such studies.'

result: The authors conclude that models remain useful in outbreak response because no individual expert consistently outperformed them, models are easily scaled and generalized, and expert interviews are time-consuming. Models offer a convenient route to quantified insights performing comparably to expert groups. The results support using models in outbreak response and suggest value in combining expert opinion with modeled forecasts.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed these conclusions, with one stating 'This research has important implications for both researchers and policy-makers' and noting the value of 'combining expert opinion with model outputs.' Another commended it as 'an interesting and important contribution.' The editor stated the evidence is 'convincing' and the work 'will be of interest' to relevant stakeholders.

result: Models performed better than experts at the lowest threshold in 4 of 5 months and marginally better at risk-ranking health zones. This may suggest experts are better at predicting simple time series than geographic distribution, and provides insight into combining models and expert opinion for future epidemics.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these interpretive findings without challenge. One reviewer noted the study 'can help to guide methods for combining expert opinion with model outputs' and another stated it provides 'insight into how models and expert opinion could be combined.' The comparative performance findings are treated as established results.
